reference.source: Standard nephrology and clinical genetics references
clinicalPearls: Caused by biallelic (homozygous or compound heterozygous) variants in COL4A3 or COL4A4, encoding the alpha-3 and alpha-4 chains of type IV collagen
Presents with progressive haematuric nephritis, often with proteinuria, that tends to progress to kidney failure earlier than in many X-linked female carriers
Sensorineural hearing loss and ocular abnormalities (such as anterior lenticonus and retinal flecks) may occur and support the diagnosis
Unlike X-linked Alport syndrome, both sexes are affected equally in the autosomal recessive form
Parents, being heterozygous carriers, may have thin basement membrane nephropathy with isolated microscopic haematuria
Kidney biopsy shows characteristic lamellation ('basket-weave') and variable thinning of the glomerular basement membrane on electron microscopy
Renin-angiotensin system blockade is the mainstay of therapy to reduce proteinuria and slow progression
reference.pathophysiology: Alport syndrome results from defective type IV collagen, the principal structural collagen of basement membranes. In the autosomal recessive form, pathogenic variants affect both copies of COL4A3 or COL4A4, so the alpha-3/alpha-4/alpha-5 collagen network of the glomerular basement membrane cannot assemble normally. The membrane becomes structurally abnormal, showing thinning and later irregular thickening and splitting (lamellation), leading to progressive glomerular leakage of blood and protein, glomerulosclerosis, tubulointerstitial fibrosis and declining renal function. The same collagen network is important in the cochlea and eye, explaining the associated sensorineural deafness and lens and retinal abnormalities. Heterozygous carriers typically have only a thinned basement membrane manifesting as benign familial haematuria.
additionalInvestigations: Urinalysis and urine protein quantification to characterise haematuria and proteinuria
Serum creatinine and eGFR to track progression
Ophthalmological assessment for lenticonus and retinopathy
Kidney biopsy with electron microscopy showing basement-membrane lamellation and thinning
Genetic testing of COL4A3 and COL4A4 with family segregation studies
redFlags: Rapidly rising creatinine or nephrotic-range proteinuria signalling accelerated progression
Advanced CKD requiring planning for renal replacement or transplantation
Rare anti-GBM disease developing after transplantation
reference.prognosis: The autosomal recessive form tends to progress to kidney failure in adolescence or early adulthood; timely renin-angiotensin blockade slows decline, and transplantation is generally successful though a small minority develop post-transplant anti-glomerular basement membrane disease.
pitfalls: Misclassifying inheritance as X-linked, which alters family risk assessment
Dismissing a carrier parent's isolated haematuria as unimportant
Missing extrarenal clues (hearing and eye findings) that point to the diagnosis
Attributing the glomerulonephritis to an acquired cause and delaying genetic testing
references: GeneReviews / KDIGO resources on Alport syndrome
management: Start renin-angiotensin system blockade with an ACE inhibitor early to reduce proteinuria and slow progression to kidney failure
Add angiotensin receptor blockade or other antiproteinuric therapy where proteinuria persists
Monitor blood pressure, proteinuria and eGFR regularly to track decline and titrate therapy
Manage chronic kidney disease complications including anaemia, mineral-bone disorder and acidosis, and control cardiovascular risk
Provide audiological surveillance with hearing amplification and ophthalmology review for lenticonus and retinopathy
Plan timely renal replacement therapy with dialysis and transplantation, watching for post-transplant anti-glomerular basement membrane disease
Offer genetic counselling and screen relatives, recognising heterozygous carriers may have thin basement membrane nephropathy
